console: We use simple examples of the main functionalities of RxJS, which can be checked in real time from our console

aboutMe.title: About me
aboutMe.description:
I have created this web tutorial with the goal of contributing to the developer community, to which I owe much of my professional growth. My gratitude to those who have selflessly shared their knowledge is immense, and it is to them that I dedicate this documentation.

RxJS is an exceptional tool for developing reactive code, although its understanding can be complex and overwhelming due to its advanced concepts. For this reason, I have aimed to make this guide as accessible and clear as possible, using simple examples that allow observing in real-time the behavior of the different operators, as well as the differences between them.

Often, a picture is worth a thousand words, and I hope this visual approach and practical perspective make learning easier. I hope you enjoy this documentation.

operators.title: RxJS operators
operators.description: The operators in RxJS are functions that allow you to work with observable data streams in a simple and efficient way. They are key tools to transform, filter, combine, and manage data in reactive applications.

welcome.title: Welcome to Play RxJS!
welcome.description: Here you will find a friendly and accessible documentation about RxJS, designed to help you understand and make the most of this amazing tool for developing reactive code. If you're new to this technology, we recommend starting with the basic concepts to get familiar with the fundamentals. Enjoy exploring and learning!

basicConcepts.title: Basic concepts
basicConcepts.description: In this section, we will talk about the basic concepts of RxJS, such as observables, observers, subscriptions, operators, and the difference between cold and hot observables. These are concepts we need to understand beforehand before diving into the wonderful world of RxJS.
basicConcepts.shortDescription: In this section, we will talk about the basic concepts of RxJS, such as observables, observers, subscriptions, operators, and the difference between cold and hot observables. These are concepts we need to understand beforehand before diving into the wonderful world of RxJS.

observableObserverSubscription.title: Observable, Observer...
observableObserverSubscription.description:
In RxJS, an observable is a data source that can emit values over time. It acts as a 'sender' of data, and any 'observer' (an object or function) can subscribe to it to receive those values. Observables allow you to manage asynchronous data flows, such as events, HTTP requests, or any kind of sequence of values.

In RxJS, an observer is an object or a function that 'listens' to the values emitted by an observable. The observer receives those values and can do something with them, like displaying them on the screen or processing them. It has three main methods: next, error, and complete.

A Subscription is the result of subscribing to an Observable using the subscribe method. It allows you to receive the values emitted by the observable and also provides methods to cancel the subscription (unsubscribe) when you no longer need to receive values.
observableObserverSubscription.example: We create an Observable that emits 1, 2 and 3 and then completes, an observer that handles each notification, and the subscription that connects them. The values are emitted synchronously, so they have all arrived by the time we call unsubscribe.

unsubscribe.title: Unsubscribe
unsubscribe.description:
In RxJS, unsubscribe is a method used to stop a subscription to an observable. Basically, it tells the observable that you no longer want to receive values emitted by it.

If you don't use unsubscribe when you no longer need the data, the observable if it's long-lived (fromEvent, interval, timer, webSocket, Subjects...), will continue running in the background, which can unnecessarily consume resources and lead to memory leaks.

In the examples on this website, we do not show the code used to unsubscribe from observables, in order to make the sections easier to read. However, internally, all observables that require it are unsubscribed from.
unsubscribe.example: Press 'Subscribe' to create a subscription to an interval: the console shows New subscription and then a number every second. Press 'Unsubscribe' to cancel it: the numbers stop and closed -> true is shown. If you press 'Subscribe' again, the previous subscription is cancelled before creating a new one, which is checked with the closed property, so the count starts again from 0.

unsubscribeSeveral.title: Unsubscribe (multiple)
unsubscribeSeveral.description:
The unsubscription of multiple observables at the same time in RxJS is done easily using a tool called Subscription. This allows you to group several subscriptions using the add method and unsubscribe from all of them at once.

This is very useful when, at a certain point in a component's lifecycle (ngOnDestroy in Angular), you want to remove all subscriptions.
unsubscribeSeveral.example: Two intervals are grouped in a single Subscription with add. Press the button to cancel both at once: the console stops receiving values.

lifecycle.title: Lifecycle: next, error and complete
lifecycle.description:
An observable talks to its subscribers through three kinds of notifications: next delivers a value and can happen any number of times, error reports a failure, and complete announces that no more values will come.

The key rule is that error and complete are final: an observable ends with one of them, never with both, and after that nothing else is delivered, even if the code keeps calling next. Operators such as catchError, retry or finalize act precisely at that moment.
lifecycle.example: We create the same order twice. Order A has stock, so it emits two steps and completes. Order B has none and fails after the first step. In both cases the value sent after the end never reaches the console, and order B never calls complete.

observableVsPromise.title: Observable vs Promise
observableVsPromise.description:
A Promise and an Observable both represent work that produces results, but they behave differently:

- Eager or lazy: a promise starts running as soon as it is created, while an observable does nothing until someone subscribes.

- One value or many: a promise settles only once, while an observable can emit any number of values over time.

- Cancellation: a promise cannot be cancelled, while an observable stops when you unsubscribe and can clean up what it was doing.

- Synchronous or asynchronous: then always runs asynchronously, while an observable can deliver its values synchronously.

To move from one to the other, use from to turn a promise into an observable, and firstValueFrom or lastValueFrom to turn an observable into a promise.
observableVsPromise.example: The promise's message appears before anything is subscribed, while the observable's message only appears when we subscribe. The second resolve is ignored, but the observable delivers 1 and 2, and it does so before the promise's then. After 1 second we unsubscribe, so 3 is never emitted and the clean-up function runs.

operatorsAndPipe.title: Operators and pipe
operatorsAndPipe.description:
An operator is a function that works with observables. There are two kinds:

- Creation operators, such as of, from or interval, create a new observable from scratch.

- Pipeable operators, such as map, filter or take, receive an observable and return a new one with a transformation applied.

The pipe method chains pipeable operators in order, so each one receives what the previous one emits. pipe never modifies the original observable: it returns a new one, so you can reuse the source to build different streams.
operatorsAndPipe.example: prices$ is created with of. With pipe we build withTax$: filter discards the prices below 10, the first map adds 21% of tax and the second one formats the result. Subscribing to prices$ shows that the original observable has not changed.

marbleDiagrams.title: Reading marble diagrams
marbleDiagrams.description:
A marble diagram shows how an operator behaves over time. It is read from left to right:

- Each horizontal line is an observable, and time runs to the right.

- Each circle (marble) is a value emitted at that moment.

- A vertical bar means that the observable completes, and an ✕ that it fails with an error.

- The box in the middle is the operator: the lines above it are its inputs and the line below is the result.

The diagram below shows map multiplying each value by 10. Every input marble produces an output marble at the same moment, and when the source completes, the result completes too.
marbleDiagrams.example: The code produces the same stream as the diagram: the values 1, 2, 3 and 4, one per second, multiplied by 10. Compare the console with the diagram: each line is a marble, and complete is the vertical bar.

coldVsHot.title: Cold and hot observables
coldVsHot.description:
A cold observable starts a new, independent execution for each subscriber, so each one receives every value from the beginning. Most observables are cold, such as those created with of, interval or ajax.

A hot observable shares a single execution among all its subscribers, so whoever subscribes late only receives the values emitted from that moment on. fromEvent and Subjects are hot, and operators such as share turn a cold observable into a hot one.

The difference matters when the execution has a cost, such as an HTTP request: with a cold observable, two subscribers make two requests.
coldVsHot.example: In both cases subscriber B arrives 1.5 seconds after A. With the cold observable, B starts its own count from 0. With the hot one, created with share, B joins the count already in progress and only receives 1 and 2.

combination.title: Combination operators
combination.description: Combination operators in RxJS allow you to work with multiple observables to combine them and create new data streams flexibly. Each operator has a specific purpose depending on how you want to combine the values from the observables.
combination.shortDescription: Combination operators in RxJS allow you to work with multiple observables to combine them and create new data streams flexibly.

combineLatest.title: combineLatest
combineLatest.description: The combineLatest operator in RxJS is a way to combine multiple observables into a single one, that emits an array with the latest value of each of them. It waits until all of them have emitted at least once and, from then on, it emits every time any of them emits.
combineLatest.example: In this example, the first combination (a0) appears once both observables have emitted. From then on, every new letter or number produces a new output.

concat.title: concat
concat.description: The concat operator in RxJS combines multiple observables sequentially, emitting the values from one until it completes, and then moves on to the next.
concat.example: obs1$ takes 2 seconds to emit, but concat waits for it to complete before subscribing to the next observables. That is why, after 2 seconds, everything is printed in order: 1, 2, a, b, 3, 4, 5.

concatAll.title: concatAll
concatAll.description: The concatAll operator in RxJS is used to 'flatten' a stream of observables sequentially. This means that if you have an observable that emits other observables, concatAll takes those observables and emits them one by one, in the order they were emitted, waiting for each one to complete before moving on to the next.
concatAll.example: The source emits three observables and concatAll subscribes to them one after another. Although obs1$ takes 2 seconds, the values keep their order: 1, 2, a, b, 3, 4, 5.

exhaust.title: exhaust
exhaust.description: The exhaust operator in RxJS is used to handle observable streams in such a way that, when a source observable emits a new observable, the operator will only listen to the first observable and any new observables emitted will be ignored until the first one completes. In other words, if the source observable continues emitting observables but is already 'working' with one, those new observables will not be listened to until the previous one completes.
exhaust.example: In this example, we can observe how the delay of the second observable prevents the third observable from executing.

forkJoin.title: forkJoin
forkJoin.description: The forkJoin operator in RxJS is used to wait for all the observables passed as arguments to complete, and when all of them have emitted their last value, it emits a single array with the last values from each of those observables.
forkJoin.example: forkJoin waits for the three observables to complete and, after 2 seconds, emits a single array with the last value of each one: [2, 'b', 5].

merge.title: merge
merge.description: The merge operator in RxJS is used to combine multiple observables and emit their values in an interleaved manner (without waiting for one to complete before listening to the next). The values are emitted in the same order in which the observables produce them, and all the observables are subscribed to and executed simultaneously.
merge.example: merge subscribes to the three observables at the same time: a, b, 3, 4 and 5 arrive straight away, and 1 and 2 two seconds later, when obs1$ emits.

mergeAll.title: mergeAll
mergeAll.description: The mergeAll operator in RxJS is used to flatten an observable stream, but in a different way compared to other operators like concatAll. With mergeAll, when an observable emits other observables, all the observables are subscribed to and executed simultaneously.
mergeAll.example: The source emits three observables and mergeAll subscribes to all of them at once, so the values of obs1$, delayed 2 seconds, arrive last.

race.title: race
race.description: The race operator in RxJS is used to race between multiple observables and emit the values of the first observable that emits something. In other words, the operator subscribes to all the observables passed to it, keeps the one that emits a value first and unsubscribes from the others.
race.example: obs2$ and obs3$ emit straight away, but obs2$ is subscribed first and wins the race: only a and b are printed, and the other observables are unsubscribed.

startWith.title: startWith
startWith.description: The startWith operator in RxJS is used to emit an initial value before any other value is emitted by the observable. In other words, you can specify a value that will be emitted first, before the observable starts emitting its own values.
startWith.example: 0 is emitted straight away, before obs1$ emits 1 and 2 two seconds later.

switchAll.title: switchAll
switchAll.description: The switchAll operator in RxJS is used to flatten an observable stream, but in a special way: when an observable emits a new observable, switchAll stops listening to the previous observable and starts listening to the new observable. In other words, it always subscribes only to the last emitted observable(s) and cancels the subscription to the previous ones.
switchAll.example: In this example, a new round starts every 2 seconds and cancels the previous one, so only the last round gets to count up to 3.

withLatestFrom.title: withLatestFrom
withLatestFrom.description: The withLatestFrom operator in RxJS is used to combine each value of the source observable with the latest value of another observable. Only the source sets the pace: when it emits, withLatestFrom takes the latest value from the second observable and combines them, while the emissions of the second observable alone produce no output. Until the second observable has emitted at least once, the values of the source are discarded.
withLatestFrom.example: In this example, second 0 is discarded because no color has been emitted yet, and the last color is repeated because the color emissions alone produce no output.

combineLatestAll.title: combineLatestAll
combineLatestAll.description: The combineLatestAll operator takes an observable that emits other observables (a higher-order observable), waits for the outer one to complete and then applies combineLatest to all the inner observables. Each time any of them emits, you get an array with the latest value of every inner observable.
combineLatestAll.example: In this example, two intervals with different speeds are combined into a single stream of arrays.

combineLatestWith.title: combineLatestWith
combineLatestWith.description: The combineLatestWith operator is the pipeable version of combineLatest. It combines the source observable with the observables you pass to it and emits an array with the latest values of all of them every time any of them emits (once all have emitted at least once).
combineLatestWith.example: In this example, we combine the readings of a temperature sensor and a humidity sensor.

concatWith.title: concatWith
concatWith.description: The concatWith operator is the pipeable version of concat. It emits all the values of the source observable and, when it completes, subscribes to the next observables one after another, in order.
concatWith.example: obs2$ and obs3$ wait for obs1$ to complete (1 second), so the output keeps the order 1, 2, a, b, 3, 4, 5.

endWith.title: endWith
endWith.description: The endWith operator is the opposite of startWith: it emits one or more values right after the source observable completes. It is useful to add a final value or signal to a data stream.
endWith.example: In this example, we simulate the steps of a process and emit Done! at the end.

exhaustAll.title: exhaustAll
exhaustAll.description: The exhaustAll operator flattens a higher-order observable by subscribing to an inner observable and ignoring every new inner observable that arrives while the current one is still active. It is the replacement for the deprecated exhaust operator.
exhaustAll.example: In this example, the delay of the second observable causes the third one to be ignored.

mergeWith.title: mergeWith
mergeWith.description: The mergeWith operator is the pipeable version of merge. It subscribes to the source and to all the observables passed as arguments at the same time, emitting their values interleaved in the order they are produced.
mergeWith.example: obs1$ is merged with obs2$ and obs3$ and the values arrive as they are produced, so 1 and 2 appear last because of their 2-second delay.

raceWith.title: raceWith
raceWith.description: The raceWith operator is the pipeable version of race. The source observable competes with the observables you pass to it: the first one to emit wins, and all the others are unsubscribed.
raceWith.example: In this example, we simulate three servers with different response times.

zip.title: zip
zip.description: The zip operator combines several observables by pairing their values by index: the first value of each one, then the second value of each one, and so on. It emits an array for each complete group and finishes when the shortest observable completes.
zip.example: In this example, we join names, ages and jobs to build a user description.

zipAll.title: zipAll
zipAll.description: The zipAll operator takes a higher-order observable, waits for it to complete and then applies zip to all the emitted inner observables, combining their values by index.
zipAll.example: zipAll waits for the outer observable to complete and pairs the values of the three inner observables by position. The slowest one, with one value per second, sets the pace.

zipWith.title: zipWith
zipWith.description: The zipWith operator is the pipeable version of zip. It pairs each value of the source with the value at the same position in the other observables. Values without a partner are never emitted.
zipWith.example: In this example, strawberry is not emitted because there is no fourth id.

conditional.title: Conditional operators
conditional.description: Conditional operators in RxJS are used to handle data streams in a conditional manner, meaning to execute logic based on whether or not a certain condition is met.
conditional.shortDescription: Conditional operators in RxJS are used to handle data streams in a conditional manner, meaning to execute logic based on whether or not a certain condition is met.

defaultIfEmpty.title: defaultIfEmpty
defaultIfEmpty.description: The defaultIfEmpty operator in RxJS is used to provide a default value when an observable does not emit any value. That is, if the observable is empty (does not emit anything), defaultIfEmpty emits the value you specify as the default.
defaultIfEmpty.example: of() completes without emitting anything, so defaultIfEmpty emits the default value: No Data.

every.title: every
every.description: The every operator in RxJS is used to check if all the values emitted by an observable satisfy a specific condition. It returns an observable that emits true if all the emitted values satisfy the condition, and false if at least one of the values does not satisfy it.
every.example: 4 is lower than 5, so not every value meets the condition and false is emitted.

find.title: find
find.description: The find operator in RxJS is used to search for the first value that satisfies a specific condition in an observable. Unlike other operators like filter, which emits all the values that satisfy the condition, find returns only the first value that satisfies the condition or undefined if no value does.
find.example: The first value greater than or equal to 5 is 5 itself, so find emits it and completes without looking at the rest.

findIndex.title: findIndex
findIndex.description: The findIndex operator in RxJS is very similar to the find operator, but instead of returning the first value that satisfies a condition, it returns the index of that value. If no value satisfies the condition, it returns -1.
findIndex.example: The first value that meets the condition (5) is at position 0, so findIndex emits 0.

isEmpty.title: isEmpty
isEmpty.description:
The isEmpty operator in RxJS is used to check if an observable does not emit any value. It returns an observable that emits:

- true if the observable does not emit any value.

- false if the observable emits at least one value.
isEmpty.example: of() completes without emitting any value, so isEmpty emits true.

sequenceEqual.title: sequenceEqual
sequenceEqual.description: The sequenceEqual operator in RxJS is used to check if two observables emit exactly the same sequence of values, in the same order.
sequenceEqual.example: Both sequences match until the last value (4 against 3), so sequenceEqual emits false.

throwIfEmpty.title: throwIfEmpty
throwIfEmpty.description: The throwIfEmpty operator makes an observable emit an error if it completes without emitting any value. If the source emits at least one value, it behaves normally. It is the opposite approach to defaultIfEmpty.
throwIfEmpty.example: The first observable emits a value and passes untouched. The second one (EMPTY) completes without emitting, so throwIfEmpty turns it into the error No data received!

creation.title: Creation operators
creation.description: In RxJS, creation operators are functions that generate observables from scratch or from other values or structures. These operators allow creating data streams that can then be processed.
creation.shortDescription: In RxJS, creation operators are functions that generate observables from scratch or from other values or structures.

ajax.title: ajax
ajax.description: The ajax operator in RxJS is a utility for making HTTP requests (such as GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) easily and handling responses as observables. It is ideal for working with data from APIs.
ajax.example: We request post number 1 from a public test API with ajax.getJSON. The response arrives already converted from JSON, and then the observable completes.

defer.title: defer
defer.description: The defer operator in RxJS is like an 'observable factory'. Its main purpose is to create a new observable when someone subscribes, instead of doing so immediately. This allows the observable to be generated on demand, ensuring it always runs with the most updated logic or data.
defer.example: The observable is subscribed twice, 2 seconds apart. Thanks to defer, the time is calculated on each subscription, so both messages show a different time.

from.title: from
from.description: The from operator is like a bridge between common JavaScript structures and the reactive world of RxJS. It converts things like arrays and promises into observables that you can use in your reactive streams.
from.example: from converts a string (it emits each letter), an array (each element) and a promise (its resolved value) into observables.

fromEvent.title: fromEvent
fromEvent.description: The fromEvent operator in RxJS converts an event into an observable. This means you can listen to events, such as mouse clicks, cursor movements, key presses, and work with them as data streams.
fromEvent.example: We listen to the keydown events of the page: type in the text field and every key you press appears in the console.

generate.title: generate
generate.description: The generate operator in RxJS is an advanced way to create observables that emit a sequence of values based on a generator function. It allows you to generate a custom data stream by specifying conditions for starting, continuing, and updating the emitted values.
generate.example: Starting at 1, the value is doubled while it is less than or equal to 64, so 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 are emitted.

iif.title: iif
iif.description: The iif operator in RxJS is a way to create a conditional observable. In other words, iif allows you to decide which observable to emit based on a condition.
iif.example: The condition 5 > 10 is false, so iif subscribes to the second observable and emits Condition is false.

interval.title: interval
interval.description: The interval operator in RxJS creates an observable that emits numeric values continuously, starting from 0, and then incrementing each time after a specific time interval.
interval.example: interval emits 0, 1, 2… every 2 seconds and never completes: press Stop to end it.

of.title: of
of.description: The of operator in RxJS creates an observable from a set of values you pass to it. These values can be any type of data, such as numbers, strings, objects, etc.
of.example: of emits the values it receives, in order and synchronously: a string, three numbers, and an object followed by an array.

range.title: range
range.description: The range operator in RxJS creates an observable that emits a sequence of consecutive numbers: you specify the initial value and how many numbers to emit, so range(1, 5) emits from 1 to 5.
range.example: range(1, 5) emits 5 consecutive numbers starting from 1, and then completes.

throwError.title: throwError
throwError.description: The throwError operator in RxJS is used to emit an error in an observable manually. This is useful when you want a data stream to stop due to a specific condition and handle an error.
throwError.example: throwError emits the error object straight away, so only the error handler runs and next never does.

timer.title: timer
timer.description: The timer operator in RxJS creates an observable that emits a value after a certain period of time (in milliseconds) and can then continue emitting values at regular intervals if specified.
timer.example: timer(2000) waits 2 seconds, emits a single value and completes.

animationFrames.title: animationFrames
animationFrames.description: The animationFrames function creates an observable that emits on every frame of the browser (using requestAnimationFrame), providing the timestamp and the elapsed time since subscription. It is perfect for creating smooth animations in a reactive way.
animationFrames.example: In this example, we move a box for 2 seconds by calculating the progress of the animation.

bindCallback.title: bindCallback
bindCallback.description: The bindCallback function converts an API based on callbacks into a function that returns an observable. When you call that function, the observable emits the values passed to the callback and then completes.
bindCallback.example: getUser uses a callback that responds after 1 second. bindCallback turns it into getUser$, a function that returns an observable that emits the user and completes.

bindNodeCallback.title: bindNodeCallback
bindNodeCallback.description: The bindNodeCallback function works like bindCallback, but for Node.js style callbacks, where the first argument is the error and the second one the result: callback(err, data). If an error arrives, the observable emits an error; otherwise it emits the result.
bindNodeCallback.example: readFile$('notes.txt') emits the content of the file, while readFile$('image.png') receives an error in the callback, so its observable emits that error.

EMPTY.title: EMPTY
EMPTY.description: EMPTY is a constant observable that does not emit any value and completes immediately. It is very useful inside flattening operators like mergeMap or switchMap to discard values, or as a return value in a catchError.
EMPTY.example: In this example, we use it to emit only the even numbers.

fromEventPattern.title: fromEventPattern
fromEventPattern.description: The fromEventPattern function creates an observable from any event API by providing two functions: one to add the handler and another to remove it. It is the generic version of fromEvent, ideal for libraries with their own event system.
fromEventPattern.example: In this example, the handler is removed automatically after 3 clicks thanks to take.

fromFetch.title: fromFetch
fromFetch.description: The fromFetch function (from rxjs/fetch) wraps the browser Fetch API in an observable. Unlike a promise, the request is cancelled automatically (AbortController) if you unsubscribe before it finishes.
fromFetch.example: We request user 1 from a public test API. If the response is correct we read its JSON; otherwise, or if the network fails, we return an object that describes the error.

NEVER.title: NEVER
NEVER.description: NEVER is a constant observable that never emits any value, never errors and never completes. It is useful for testing, for keeping a stream alive or for combining it with operators like timeout.
NEVER.example: The first NEVER only emits the value added with startWith and never completes. The second one shows a typical use: timeout fails after 2 seconds because NEVER emits nothing, and catchError turns that error into a message.

scheduled.title: scheduled
scheduled.description: The scheduled function converts an array, promise or iterable into an observable whose emissions are controlled by a scheduler. It lets you decide when values are delivered: synchronously, as a microtask (asapScheduler) or as a macrotask (asyncScheduler).
scheduled.example: In this example, the synchronous code ends before any value is emitted.

webSocket.title: webSocket
webSocket.description: The webSocket function (from rxjs/webSocket) creates a WebSocketSubject: a subject that lets you send messages with next and receive them by subscribing. The connection opens when the first subscriber arrives and closes automatically when the last one unsubscribes.
webSocket.example: We connect to a public echo server that returns every message we send. The server first sends a welcome message of its own (Request served by…) and then the echo of our two messages. With take(3) we receive those 3 messages and the connection closes.

error.title: Error handling operators
error.description: The error handling operators in RxJS are used to handle, recover, or react to errors that may occur in the data flow of an Observable. These operators allow your application to continue running when an error occurs, giving you control over how to manage it.
error.shortDescription: Error handling operators in RxJS are used to handle, recover, or react to errors that may occur in the data flow of an Observable.

catchError.title: catchError
catchError.description:
The catchError operator in RxJS is used to capture an error that occurs in an Observable and allow you to handle it in a controlled way, so that the error does not reach the subscriber. The source that failed does not continue: the stream carries on with the Observable you return.

When an Observable emits an error, catchError gives you the opportunity to recover from that error. You can return a new Observable to emit instead of the error, or simply perform an action when the error occurs.
catchError.example: throwError fails straight away. catchError logs the message and replaces the error with an observable that emits an empty array, which is what reaches the subscriber.

retry.title: retry
retry.description: The retry operator in RxJS is used to reattempt the execution of an Observable in case an error occurs. This operator allows you to automatically retry the data flow a specified number of times before it ultimately fails.
retry.example: In this example, we will see in the console how the URL is retried once after the error.

onErrorResumeNext.title: onErrorResumeNext
onErrorResumeNext.description: The onErrorResumeNext function subscribes to a list of observables one after another, moving on to the next one when the current one completes or fails. Errors are silently ignored, so the final observer never receives them.
onErrorResumeNext.example: failing$ emits 1 and 2 and fails on its third value. The error is ignored and the next observables run: the second one also fails and is ignored, and the third emits a and b. The final observer only receives complete, never the error.

retryWhen.title: retryWhen
retryWhen.description: The retryWhen operator lets you decide how and when to retry after an error, using an observable of errors. It is deprecated: nowadays retry accepts a configuration object such as retry({ count: 3, delay: 1000 }).
retryWhen.example: In this example, the request fails twice and succeeds on the third attempt, waiting 1 second between retries.

onErrorResumeNextWith.title: onErrorResumeNextWith
onErrorResumeNextWith.description: The onErrorResumeNextWith operator is the pipeable version of onErrorResumeNext. When the source completes or fails, it moves on to the next observable you pass to it. Errors are silently ignored, so the final observer never receives them.
onErrorResumeNextWith.example: In this example, failing$ throws an error on its third value and backup$ takes over.

filtering.title: Filtering operators
filtering.description: In RxJS, filtering operators are used to filter the items emitted by an observable, allowing only those that meet a specific condition to pass through. These operators are useful for working with data streams, ensuring that only the relevant values are processed.
filtering.shortDescription: In RxJS, filtering operators are used to filter the items emitted by an observable, allowing only those that meet a specific condition to pass through.

audit.title: audit
audit.description: The audit operator in RxJS is used to control the emission of values from an observable, based on another observable that acts as a 'time window'.
audit.example: Click the button several times. The first click starts a 2-second wait and, when it ends, audit emits the last click of that time, so the console tells you which click got through. The clicks made during the wait do not restart it.

auditTime.title: auditTime
auditTime.description: The auditTime operator in RxJS is a simple way to control the frequency at which values are emitted by an observable. It works similarly to audit, but instead of relying on an external observable, it uses a fixed time period that you define.
auditTime.example: Click the button several times quickly. auditTime waits 2 seconds from the first click and then emits only the last one: of clicks 1, 2 and 3, only click 3 is emitted.

debounce.title: debounce
debounce.description: The debounce operator in RxJS is useful for controlling how many values from an observable are processed, especially when the values arrive quickly (like key presses or clicks). This operator waits for a period of time after receiving a value, and only emits that value if no new values are received during that time.
debounce.example: In this example, we will log the last key pressed to the console.

debounceTime.title: debounceTime
debounceTime.description: The debounceTime operator in RxJS is very similar to debounce, but instead of using an observable to define the wait time, it simply uses a fixed time period.
debounceTime.example: Type in the text field: a key is only logged when you stop typing for 1 second, so you see the last key pressed.

distinct.title: distinct
distinct.description: The distinct operator in RxJS is used to filter duplicate values that an observable may emit. It only emits unique values (i.e., those that do not repeat) and discards the values that have already been emitted.
distinct.example: Repeated numbers are discarded wherever they appear, so each number from 1 to 8 is emitted only once.

distinctUntilChanged.title: distinctUntilChanged
distinctUntilChanged.description: The distinctUntilChanged operator in RxJS is used to filter consecutive repeated values in a data stream. It emits a value only if it is different from the last emitted value.
distinctUntilChanged.example: Only consecutive repetitions are discarded: 2, 2 becomes a single 2, but a 2 that appears again later is emitted.

distinctUntilKeyChanged.title: distinctUntilKeyChanged
distinctUntilKeyChanged.description: The distinctUntilKeyChanged operator in RxJS is very similar to distinctUntilChanged, but it is used when the values emitted by the observable are objects or contain properties, and you want to filter out values that have not changed in a specific property.
distinctUntilKeyChanged.example: Users are compared by their name property: the second John and the second Mari are discarded because they come right after a user with the same name.

elementAt.title: elementAt
elementAt.description: The elementAt operator in RxJS is used to get a specific value at a given position from a data stream emitted by an observable.
elementAt.example: elementAt(3) emits the element at position 3, counting from 0, which is the second Mari.

filter.title: filter
filter.description: The filter operator in RxJS is used to filter the values emitted by an observable, allowing only the values that meet a specific condition to pass through.
filter.example: In this example, we filter for users who are older than 3 years and have different names.

first.title: first
first.description: The first operator in RxJS is used to emit only the first value from an observable that meets a specific condition, or simply the first value if no condition is defined. If the observable does not emit any value, it can throw an error or emit a default value if specified.
first.example: first emits the first user older than 3, Mari, and completes.

ignoreElements.title: ignoreElements
ignoreElements.description: The ignoreElements operator in RxJS is used to ignore all values emitted by an observable. This operator does not emit anything, but it does pass errors or the signal that the observable has completed.
ignoreElements.example: The three values are ignored and only the completion signal arrives, so only complete is printed.

last.title: last
last.description: The last operator in RxJS is used to emit only the last value from an observable that meets a specific condition. If the observable does not emit any value, it can throw an error or emit a default value if specified.
last.example: In this example, we force it to not find any value in order to see the default value.

sample.title: sample
sample.description: The sample operator in RxJS is used to take the last value emitted by an observable at specific moments defined by another observable that acts as a 'time source'.
sample.example: The interval emits one number per second and, every 5 seconds, sample takes the last one emitted so far: 4, 9, 14…

sampleTime.title: sampleTime
sampleTime.description: The sampleTime operator in RxJS is used to take the last value emitted by an observable at fixed time intervals. Each time the specified time period passes, the operator emits the last value produced up to that moment.
sampleTime.example: Every 3 seconds, sampleTime takes the last value emitted by the interval: 2, 5, 8…

single.title: single
single.description: The single operator in RxJS is used to ensure that an observable emits only one value, and that value must meet a specific condition (if defined). If the observable emits more than one value or none at all, an error will be thrown.
single.example: In obs1$ only 5 meets the condition, so it is emitted. In obs2$ both 4 and 5 meet it, so single throws an error.

skip.title: skip
skip.description: The skip operator in RxJS is a tool used to ignore a certain number of initial values emitted by an observable. After 'skipping' these values, it starts passing the subsequent values that are emitted.
skip.example: The first 2 values (1 and 2) are skipped, and 3 and 4 are emitted.

skipLast.title: skipLast
skipLast.description: The skipLast operator in RxJS is very similar to skip, but instead of ignoring values at the beginning, it ignores the last values emitted by an observable. This means it allows all values to pass except for the last n.
skipLast.example: skipLast(2) waits to know which values are the last ones: it discards 3 and 4 and emits 1 and 2.

skipUntil.title: skipUntil
skipUntil.description: The skipUntil operator in RxJS is used to ignore values emitted by an observable until another observable emits a value. At that point, it starts allowing the values from the original observable to pass through.
skipUntil.example: The values of the interval are ignored until the second interval emits for the first time, after 3 seconds. From then on all of them are emitted: 2, 3, 4…

skipWhile.title: skipWhile
skipWhile.description: The skipWhile operator in RxJS is used to ignore values emitted by an observable while a condition is met. As soon as the condition is no longer met, it starts passing the values emitted by the observable.
skipWhile.example: Values are ignored while they are less than 5. From 5 onwards, all of them are emitted.

take.title: take
take.description: The take operator in RxJS is used to limit the number of values that an observable can emit. Once the observable has emitted the specified number of values, it completes automatically.
take.example: Only the first 5 values of the interval (0 to 4) are taken, and then the observable completes.

takeLast.title: takeLast
takeLast.description: The takeLast operator in RxJS is used to take the last n emitted values from an observable, after the observable has completed.
takeLast.example: When the observable completes, takeLast(2) emits its last two values: 3 and 4.

takeUntil.title: takeUntil
takeUntil.description: The takeUntil operator in RxJS is used to take values emitted by an observable until another observable emits a value. When that other observable emits, the flow of the original observable completes, meaning it stops emitting more values.
takeUntil.example: The values of the interval are emitted until the second interval emits, after 3 seconds. At that moment the observable completes.

takeWhile.title: takeWhile
takeWhile.description: The takeWhile operator in RxJS is used to take values emitted by an observable while a condition is met. When the condition is no longer met, the observable completes and stops emitting more values.
takeWhile.example: Values are emitted while they are less than 5. When 5 arrives, the condition fails and the observable completes.

throttle.title: throttle
throttle.description: The throttle operator in RxJS is used to limit the emission frequency of an observable, ensuring that only one value is emitted within a specified time interval, and any values that arrive before the interval passes are ignored.
throttle.example: In this example, click the button several times quickly: the first click is accepted and the following ones are ignored for 2 seconds.

throttleTime.title: throttleTime
throttleTime.description: The throttleTime operator in RxJS is used to limit the emission frequency of an observable, in a similar way to throttle, but in a more simplified manner. With throttleTime, you can specify a time interval during which only one emission will be allowed, ignoring all intermediate emissions.
throttleTime.example: In this example, click the button several times quickly: the first click is accepted and the following ones are ignored for 2 seconds.

mathematical.title: Mathematical operators
mathematical.description: Mathematical operators in RxJS are used to perform calculations and mathematical transformations on the values emitted by an observable. These operators allow summing, averaging, or finding minimum or maximum values within a data stream.
mathematical.shortDescription: Mathematical operators in RxJS are used to perform calculations and mathematical transformations on the values emitted by an observable.

count.title: count
count.description: The count operator in RxJS is used to count the number of values emitted by an observable that meet a specific condition. If no condition is provided, it counts all emitted values.
count.example: count counts how many values are greater than 3 (4 and 5), so it emits 2.

max.title: max
max.description: The max operator in RxJS is used to find the maximum value emitted by an observable. This operator compares all emitted values and returns the highest one.
max.example: max emits 5, the highest value, when the observable completes.

min.title: min
min.description: The min operator in RxJS is used to find the minimum value emitted by an observable. This operator compares all emitted values and returns the lowest one.
min.example: min emits 1, the lowest value, when the observable completes.

reduce.title: reduce
reduce.description: The reduce operator in RxJS is used to accumulate the values emitted by an observable, similar to how reduce works in JavaScript arrays. It takes all the emitted values and combines them into a single final value.
reduce.example: reduce adds up all the values starting from 0 and emits the total, 15, only when the observable completes.

multicasting.title: Multicasting operators
multicasting.description: Multicasting operators in RxJS are used to share a single stream of values among multiple subscribers, so the values emitted by the observable are not repeated for each subscriber. This optimizes performance by preventing values from being emitted multiple times for each subscriber.
multicasting.shortDescription: Multicasting operators in RxJS are used to share a single stream of values among multiple subscribers, so the values emitted by the observable are not repeated for each subscriber.

connect.title: connect
connect.description: The connect operator shares a single subscription to the source inside a function you provide. That function receives a multicast observable that you can subscribe to as many times as you need, and the source only starts once all of those subscriptions are in place, so no value is lost. It is the modern replacement for multicast and publish when the sharing is only needed inside the pipe.
connect.example: In this example, the source is used twice, but the tap runs only once per value.

share.title: share
share.description: The share operator in RxJS is a form of multicast that allows a single data stream emitted by an observable to be shared among multiple subscribers, without each subscriber receiving its own emissions. This prevents the observable from being executed more than once, optimizing performance.
share.example: The second subscriber arrives at 5 seconds and shares the same execution: it does not receive the previous values and starts with the current one.

shareReplay.title: shareReplay
shareReplay.description: The shareReplay operator in RxJS is similar to the share operator, but with a key difference: it caches the last emitted values from the observable and replays them to new subscribers. It is useful when you want new subscribers to receive the latest emitted values without re-executing the entire data flow.
shareReplay.example: The second subscriber arrives at 5 seconds and first receives the last 3 stored values (2, 3 and 4). Then it continues with the shared execution.

connectable.title: connectable
connectable.description: The connectable function creates an observable that does not start emitting until you call connect(), sharing a single execution among all its subscribers. It is the modern replacement for publish, multicast and ConnectableObservable.
connectable.example: In this example, both subscribers are ready, but nothing is emitted until we connect 2 seconds later.

multicast.title: multicast
multicast.description: The multicast operator shares a single execution of the source through a Subject that you provide, returning a ConnectableObservable that starts when you call connect(). It is deprecated in favour of connectable and share.
multicast.example: In this example, the tap runs only once per value although there are two subscribers.

publishBehavior.title: publishBehavior
publishBehavior.description: The publishBehavior operator is like multicast with a BehaviorSubject: it needs an initial value and new subscribers receive the latest emitted value immediately. It is deprecated in favour of connectable with a BehaviorSubject.
publishBehavior.example: Subscriber A receives the initial value -1 straight away. Subscriber B arrives 1.5 seconds later and immediately receives the latest value, 0, before continuing with the following ones.

publishLast.title: publishLast
publishLast.description: The publishLast operator is like multicast with an AsyncSubject: it shares the source but only emits the last value, and only when the source completes. It is deprecated in favour of connectable with an AsyncSubject.
publishLast.example: The source emits 0 to 3, but both subscribers only receive the last value, 3, when the source completes.

publishReplay.title: publishReplay
publishReplay.description: The publishReplay operator is like multicast with a ReplaySubject: it shares the source and replays the last N values to late subscribers. It is deprecated in favour of shareReplay or connectable.
publishReplay.example: Subscriber B arrives at 3.5 seconds and first receives the last 2 values replayed (1 and 2). Then it continues with the rest, like A.

refCount.title: refCount
refCount.description: The refCount operator turns a ConnectableObservable into an observable that connects automatically when the first subscriber arrives and disconnects when the last one leaves. It is deprecated: the share operator does the same in a single step.
refCount.example: The source starts when A subscribes. B joins 1.5 seconds later and shares the same execution. When both unsubscribe, the source stops and no more source messages appear.

publish.title: publish
publish.description: The publish operator turns an observable into a ConnectableObservable: it shares a single execution among its subscribers through a Subject and does not start emitting until you call connect(). It is deprecated in favour of connectable and share.
publish.example: In this example, the interval only starts when we press the button.

transformation.title: Transformation operators
transformation.description: RxJS transformation operators are tools that let you change (or 'transform') the data that flows through an observable stream. Imagine you have a stream of values, like numbers or objects, and you want to modify, filter, or reshape these values before they reach the final observer.
transformation.shortDescription: RxJS transformation operators are tools for modifying the data flowing through an observable.

buffer.title: buffer
buffer.description: The buffer operator in RxJS collects emissions from a source observable into an array and delivers them together when another observable, known as the trigger, emits a value. It is useful for grouping values over time intervals or in response to events.
buffer.example: In this example, we count the clicks made on a button every 3 seconds.

bufferCount.title: bufferCount
bufferCount.description: The bufferCount operator in RxJS is used to group emissions from an observable into 'buffers' or fixed-size batches and emit them as an array.
bufferCount.example: In this example, we will emit the array after making 5 clicks.

bufferTime.title: bufferTime
bufferTime.description: The bufferTime operator in RxJS groups the emissions of an observable over a fixed period of time and emits them together as an array.
bufferTime.example: In this example, we display the array generated by the interval emission every 3 seconds.

bufferWhen.title: bufferWhen
bufferWhen.description: The bufferWhen operator in RxJS allows you to collect values emitted by a source observable into 'buffers' (arrays) and emit those buffers when a condition is met. The condition for closing each buffer is defined by a function that returns an observable. When this observable emits a value, the buffer is closed, and a new one begins.
bufferWhen.example: The interval collects its values in a buffer. Each click emits that buffer as an array and starts a new one, so you see the values emitted since the previous click. The interval counts from 0 when you press Run, and if you click twice within a second you get an empty array.

concatMap.title: concatMap
concatMap.description: The concatMap operator in RxJS is used to queue up observables one after another, ensuring they run in sequence. When concatMap receives a value, it maps that value to a new observable (like a network request or a timer) and waits for it to complete before moving to the next one.
concatMap.example: In this example, we merge the observable from a button click with the observable from an interval. Each time we click the button, we can see in the console how the observables are concatenated in an orderly manner, respecting their sequence.

exhaustMap.title: exhaustMap
exhaustMap.description: The exhaustMap operator in RxJS is used to handle asynchronous data streams, ensuring that only one operation is processed at a time and ignoring any new actions while the current operation is still in progress.
exhaustMap.example: Click the button several times quickly. The first click starts a request that takes 2 seconds, and the clicks made in the meantime are ignored: they appear in the console but get no response. Once the request finishes, the next click starts a new one.

expand.title: expand
expand.description: The expand operator in RxJS is used to generate a stream of values recursively, meaning it allows each emitted value to generate new values based on a defined logic.
expand.example: In this example, we add 10 to each emitted value and repeat the operation 5 times.

groupBy.title: groupBy
groupBy.description: The groupBy operator in RxJS is used to group elements emitted by an observable based on a key that you define. Think of it as a way to separate a data stream into different 'boxes' based on certain characteristics.
groupBy.example: In this example, we group the species into different arrays, through a mergeMap and a toArray.

map.title: map
map.description: The map operator in RxJS applies a function to each value emitted by an observable and returns an observable that emits the transformed values.
map.example: In this example, we transform the user's name using the map operator and use the array's map method to update the name of each item within it.

mapTo.title: mapTo
mapTo.description: The mapTo operator in RxJS replaces each value emitted by an observable with a specific value you provide.
mapTo.example: In this example, with the mapTo operator, we replace all values from the observable with the value strawberry.

mergeMap.title: mergeMap
mergeMap.description: The mergeMap operator in RxJS is used to transform the values emitted by an observable into other observables and then 'flattens' or combines all those emissions into a single data stream. This is useful when you want to perform multiple asynchronous operations at the same time and combine their results as they arrive.
mergeMap.example: In this example, we launch three simulated requests with different durations. All of them run at the same time, so the responses arrive in the order they finish (2, 3, 1), not in the order they were requested.

mergeMapTo.title: mergeMapTo
mergeMapTo.description: The mergeMapTo operator in RxJS is used to replace each value emitted by an observable with a different observable that you specify, and it then 'flattens' all the results into a single output stream.
mergeMapTo.example: In this example, each ping is answered with the same pong observable. Unlike mergeMap, the emitted value is not used, and the pongs overlap because mergeMapTo does not wait for the previous one to finish.

mergeScan.title: mergeScan
mergeScan.description: The RxJS mergeScan operator is like a combination of a reduce and a mergeMap, but it is applied to a stream of data (an observable) instead of a static collection like an array. It is used when you want to maintain an accumulative state as values are emitted from an observable, while simultaneously generating new observables from each emitted value.
mergeScan.example: In this example, we cumulatively sum the numbers from the observable.

pairwise.title: pairwise
pairwise.description: The RxJS pairwise operator is a simple operator that groups consecutive values emitted by an observable into pairs. Each time the observable emits a new value, this operator takes the previous and the current values and combines them into a two-element array.
pairwise.example: In this example, we can see how the last two emitted values are concatenated into an array.

partition.title: partition
partition.description:
The RxJS partition operator is a simple way to split a stream of data (observable) into two parts based on a condition. Essentially, it separates the emitted values into two different observables:

- One observable for the values that meet the condition.

- Another observable for the values that do not meet the condition.
partition.example: In this example, we group the animals into two categories, those that are cats and those that are not.

pluck.title: pluck
pluck.description: The RxJS pluck operator is a simple way to extract a specific value from an object emitted by an observable. Essentially, it works like directly accessing a property by its name, but within the context of a data stream.
pluck.example: In this example, we will log the names of the animals from our observable to the console.

scan.title: scan
scan.description: The scan operator in RxJS is very similar to the reduce function of arrays, but it applies to data streams. Essentially, it accumulates a value over time as new values arrive in the stream.
scan.example: In this example, we cumulatively sum the values of the observable.

switchMap.title: switchMap
switchMap.description: The switchMap operator in RxJS is used to switch from one observable to a new one whenever a new value is emitted by the original observable. When this happens, switchMap cancels (or 'unsubscribes' from) the previous observable and only listens to the latest one.
switchMap.example: In this example, we merge the observable from a button click with the observable from an interval. Each time we click the button, we can see in the console how the previous observable is canceled.

window.title: window
window.description: The RxJS window operator divides a data stream (observable) into sub-observables, called 'windows'. Each window groups the elements emitted by the original stream according to a defined criterion and closes when a specific event occurs.
window.example: In this example, we group numbers into 'windows' of three.

windowCount.title: windowCount
windowCount.description: The RxJS windowCount operator divides a data stream (observable) into sub-observables (windows) based on a fixed number of emissions. In other words, each 'window' groups a specific number of emitted values.
windowCount.example: A new window starts every 2 values and each one collects up to 3 values: [1, 2, 3], [3, 4, 5] and [5, 6]. The last window, [], opens after the sixth value, just when the source completes, so it closes empty.

windowTime.title: windowTime
windowTime.description: The RxJS windowTime operator divides a data stream (observable) into 'fixed-time windows'. Each window is a sub-observable that groups the values emitted during a specific time interval.
windowTime.example: In this example, we group the values emitted by the interval into 3-second windows.

windowWhen.title: windowWhen
windowWhen.description: The RxJS windowWhen operator divides a data stream (observable) into windows that close and open based on a custom criterion. You decide when a window should close and a new one should open using a function that generates observables.
windowWhen.example: In this example, we emit values from an interval that opens and closes every 3 seconds.

bufferToggle.title: bufferToggle
bufferToggle.description: The bufferToggle operator in RxJS allows you to collect values emitted by an observable into buffers (arrays) and emit those buffers based on signals from other observables. It works by opening and closing buffers based on events triggered by opening and closing observables.
bufferToggle.example: Press 'Start' to open a buffer and 'Stop' to close it: you will see the values that the interval emitted in between. The interval counts from 0 when you press Run, so the numbers keep growing, and if you close the buffer before a second has passed you get an empty array. 'Stop' does nothing if there is no open buffer.

windowToggle.title: windowToggle
windowToggle.description:
The RxJS windowToggle operator divides a data stream (observable) into windows that open and close based on two observables:

- Opener (openings): An observable that indicates when to open a new window.

- Closer (closings): A function that generates an observable to decide when to close the window.
windowToggle.example: In this example, we emit the values from the interval, opening a new window every 3 seconds and closing it after 2 seconds.

concatMapTo.title: concatMapTo
concatMapTo.description: The concatMapTo operator maps every value of the source to the same inner observable and subscribes to them in order, waiting for each one to complete. It is deprecated: use concatMap(() => obs$).
concatMapTo.example: Each click queues the same count from 0 to 2. If you click several times quickly the counts do not mix: each one waits for the previous one to finish.

switchMapTo.title: switchMapTo
switchMapTo.description: The switchMapTo operator maps every value of the source to the same inner observable, cancelling the previous one each time. It is deprecated: use switchMap(() => obs$).
switchMapTo.example: Each click restarts the same interval from 0 and cancels the previous count, so if you keep clicking the count never gets far.

switchScan.title: switchScan
switchScan.description: The switchScan operator combines scan and switchMap: it keeps an accumulator, but the accumulator function returns an observable. If a new value arrives before that observable emits, the previous one is cancelled and the last accumulated value is used.
switchScan.example: A value arrives every 400 ms (0 to 4). Odd values answer after 100 ms and even values after 600 ms, so an even one is cancelled when the next value arrives, except the last one. That is why only the totals 1 (0 + 1), 4 (1 + 3) and 8 (4 + 4) are emitted.

utility.title: Utility operators
utility.description: The utility operators in RxJS are tools that help control and manage data streams (Observables) more efficiently, without directly transforming the values passing through them. They are like 'helpers' for common tasks, such as debugging, subscription, or flow manipulation.
utility.shortDescription: Utility operators in RxJS are tools that help control and manage data streams (Observables) more efficiently, without directly transforming the values that pass through them.

delay.title: delay
delay.description: The delay operator in RxJS is like a 'clock' that delays the emissions of values from an Observable for a period of time that you determine.
delay.example: The value is emitted 2 seconds after subscribing.

delayWhen.title: delayWhen
delayWhen.description: The delayWhen operator in RxJS is like delay, but more flexible. Instead of delaying a value for a fixed time, it allows delaying it using another Observable to decide when it should be emitted.
delayWhen.example: Each value is delayed by its own timer: error waits 2 seconds and success does not wait, so success arrives first even though it was emitted second.

dematerialize.title: dematerialize
dematerialize.description: The dematerialize operator in RxJS converts the 'notifications' of an Observable (which are encapsulated as special objects) back into normal values or events.
dematerialize.example: materialize turns the values into notifications and dematerialize turns them back into normal values, so 1, 2 and 3 are printed as usual.

finalize.title: finalize
finalize.description: The finalize operator in RxJS is used to execute an action when an Observable finishes (whether completing or encountering an error). It acts like a 'cleaner' that ensures something happens at the end of the data flow, regardless of whether everything was successful or there was an error.
finalize.example: After emitting 1, 2 and 3 the observable completes, and then the finalize callback runs.

materialize.title: materialize
materialize.description: The materialize operator in RxJS converts the emissions of an Observable into notifications. That is, instead of emitting just the values, the Observable emits objects that represent flow events like next, error, or complete.
materialize.example: Each value is emitted as a Notification object with kind 'N' (next), and the completion as one with kind 'C' (complete).

repeat.title: repeat
repeat.description: The repeat operator in RxJS is used to re-emit an Observable after it has completed, repeating its flow the number of times you specify.
repeat.example: When of(1, 2, 3) completes, repeat(2) subscribes again, so the sequence is emitted twice.

tap.title: tap
tap.description: The tap operator in RxJS is very useful for intercepting and observing the emissions of an Observable without modifying its values. It's like a 'spy' that allows you to perform secondary actions (such as logging to the console) in the data flow, but without affecting the data passing through the Observable.
tap.example: tap logs each value as it passes, without changing it, and then the subscriber receives it.

timeInterval.title: timeInterval
timeInterval.description: The timeInterval operator in RxJS is used to measure the time elapsed between the emissions of an Observable. It's like a clock that tells you how much time has passed between each emission of a value.
timeInterval.example: Each value comes with the milliseconds elapsed since the previous one, around 1000.

timeout.title: timeout
timeout.description: The timeout operator in RxJS is used to set a time limit on an Observable. If the Observable does not emit a value within the specified time, it emits an error or a default action.
timeout.example: In this example, we create an observable using the timer operator, but since the timeout operator has a shorter time interval, we will force the error.

timestamp.title: timestamp
timestamp.description: The timestamp operator in RxJS is used to add a timestamp to each value emitted by an Observable. This timestamp indicates the exact moment (in milliseconds since the Unix epoch) when the value was emitted.
timestamp.example: Each value comes with the moment it was emitted, in milliseconds since 1970.

toArray.title: toArray
toArray.description: The toArray operator in RxJS is used to collect all the values emitted by an Observable and store them in an array. Once the Observable has completed its emission of values, toArray returns that array with all the emitted values.
toArray.example: In this example, we take only 5 values emitted by an interval and group them into an array.

firstValueFrom.title: firstValueFrom
firstValueFrom.description: The firstValueFrom function converts an observable into a Promise that resolves with the first emitted value and then unsubscribes. It is the modern replacement for toPromise() and works great with async/await.
firstValueFrom.example: The promise resolves with the first value of the interval, after 1 second, and the interval is unsubscribed automatically.

lastValueFrom.title: lastValueFrom
lastValueFrom.description: The lastValueFrom function converts an observable into a Promise that resolves with the last value once the observable completes. Be careful: if the observable never completes, the promise never resolves.
lastValueFrom.example: The promise waits for the interval to emit its 4 values and complete, and resolves with the last one, 3.

observeOn.title: observeOn
observeOn.description: The observeOn operator re-emits every notification of the source using a scheduler. With asyncScheduler, values that would be delivered synchronously are delivered asynchronously, after the current code finishes.
observeOn.example: With asyncScheduler the values are delivered after the synchronous code, so the second message is printed before 1, 2 and 3.

subscribeOn.title: subscribeOn
subscribeOn.description: The subscribeOn operator controls when the subscription to the source happens, using a scheduler. Unlike observeOn, it affects the moment of subscription, not the delivery of each value.
subscribeOn.example: In this example, the B values are printed first because the subscription to A is delayed.

subjects.welcome: Discover how to easily manage the state changes in the data models of any reactive application using Subjects. These tools allow you to keep all components and services always updated simultaneously, in a simple and efficient way!.
subjects.title: Subjects
subjects.description: In RxJS, Subjects are a key concept that combines two roles: that of an observable (something that emits values) and that of an observer (something that receives values). This means you can use them both to receive data and to emit it to other observers. They enable the multicast of values to many observers. While simple Observables are unicast (each subscribed Observer owns an independent execution of the Observable), subjects are multicast.
subjects.shortDescription: In RxJS, Subjects are a key concept that combines two roles: that of an observable (something that emits values) and that of an observer (something that receives values).

behaviorSubject.title: BehaviorSubject
behaviorSubject.description:
The BehaviorSubject is a special type of subject in RxJS that always has an initial value and also remembers the last emitted value. This means that any new subscriber automatically receives the most recent value, even if they subscribe after that value has been emitted.

We can access its content without needing to subscribe by using the getValue method.
behaviorSubject.example: In this example, we create a BehaviorSubject, and its content is immediately propagated to all subscriptions (initial value). We also log its content to the console using the getValue method and then update its age using the next method, which propagates the change, allowing us to see the new value in the subscription.

replaySubject.title: ReplaySubject
replaySubject.description: The ReplaySubject in RxJS is a type of Subject that stores a history of emitted values and, when a new subscriber joins, it replays all the values that have been emitted up until that point. You can configure how many previous values you want the ReplaySubject to remember.
replaySubject.example: The interval sends its values, from 0 to 4, to the ReplaySubject, which stores the last 2. After 5 seconds we subscribe and immediately receive the stored values: 3 and 4.

subject.title: Subject
subject.description: The Subject is a special type of observable in RxJS that is also an observer: you can push values into it with next and it delivers them to all its current subscribers. It does not require an initial value and does not remember past values, so a new subscriber only receives what is emitted after subscribing. If you need the last value, use a BehaviorSubject or a ReplaySubject.
subject.example: In this example, through a click event and based on the content of the variable user, we either create the user or increment their age, and through the next function, we propagate the change.

asyncSubject.title: AsyncSubject
asyncSubject.description: The AsyncSubject is a type of subject that only emits the last value it received, and only when it completes. Subscribers that arrive after completion also receive that last value. It is similar to how a Promise works.
asyncSubject.example: Values 1, 2 and 3 are pushed, but nothing is emitted until complete() is called 1.5 seconds later. Then A receives the last value, 3, and B, which subscribes afterwards, also receives it.

realLife.title: Real-life examples
realLife.description: In this section, we will present a series of practical examples that might be encountered in real-life situations and demonstrate how to address them using the concepts and techniques outlined in this RxJS documentation.
realLife.shortDescription: In this section, we will present a series of practical examples that may arise in real-life situations and demonstrate how to address them using the concepts and techniques covered in this RxJS documentation.

filterUsersMap.title: Filter (map)
filterUsersMap.description: In this example, we explain how to filter a list of users obtained through an HTTP GET service. We will use the RxJS map operator in combination with the array's filter function to apply filtering efficiently.
filterUsersMap.example: The simulated request returns all the users, and map filters the array so that only those who earn at least 30000 and are older than 39 remain: John.

filterUsersMergeMapFilter.title: Filter (mergeMap, filter)
filterUsersMergeMapFilter.description: In this example, we present an alternative for filtering users using the mergeMap and filter operators. With the first operator, we transform the array of users into individual emissions, which allows the application of the filter operator. Subsequently, we use the toArray operator to reassemble an array with the filtered users. From an efficiency standpoint, I consider the previous example to be more optimal; however, from a didactic perspective, this approach is very useful for practicing the concepts learned in this documentation.
filterUsersMergeMapFilter.example: mergeMap emits the users one by one, filter keeps those who earn at least 30000 and are older than 39, and toArray groups them back into an array.

mergeUsersHobbiesforkJoinConcatMap.title: Merge (data API)
mergeUsersHobbiesforkJoinConcatMap.description: In this example, the integration of the user list with the hobbies list is performed through the name field. For this purpose, the forkJoin operator is used, which waits for both requests to complete and emits their results together. Then, the map operator enriches each user with their hobbies, using the map and find functions of arrays to establish the association.
mergeUsersHobbiesforkJoinConcatMap.example: forkJoin waits for both requests (the users take 2 seconds) and map adds to each user their hobbies, matching them by name.

filterAndmergeUsersHobbies.title: Filter and merge (data API)
filterAndmergeUsersHobbies.description: In this example, the integration of a user filtered by the name field from the user list with the hobbies list is carried out. Then, using the map operator and the find function, an object is created that contains the data of the user and their respective hobbies.
filterAndmergeUsersHobbies.example: From the users we keep John, and when both requests finish we combine his data with his hobbies in a single object.

searchApi.title: Search (data API)
searchApi.description: In this example, we will implement search in an API using the input event on a text field. We use the debounceTime operator to wait 1 second after the last keystroke, in order to avoid multiple calls to the API. The filter operator ensures that the search only runs when the text has at least 2 characters, and switchMap cancels any previous request that is still pending.
searchApi.example: Type the name of a Pokémon: the search starts 1 second after you stop typing and only with 2 or more characters. A name that does not exist shows Pokémon not found.

flatteningOperators.title: mergeMap, concatMap, switchMap or exhaustMap?
flatteningOperators.description:
mergeMap, concatMap, switchMap and exhaustMap all turn each value into an observable, such as an HTTP request. What changes is what they do when a new value arrives before the previous request has finished:

- mergeMap runs all of them at the same time. Use it when the requests are independent, such as deleting several items.

- concatMap queues them and runs them one after another, in order. Use it when the order matters, such as saving successive changes.

- switchMap cancels the previous one and keeps only the last. Use it when only the latest result matters, such as a search box.

- exhaustMap ignores new values until the current one finishes. Use it to avoid duplicates, such as a login or payment button clicked twice.
flatteningOperators.example: Each click on the button simulates a save request that takes 1.5 seconds, and the four operators receive the same clicks. Click 3 times quickly: mergeMap saves the 3 at the same time, concatMap saves them one after another, switchMap only saves the last one and exhaustMap only the first.
